description: The Christmas-tree scent of Vermont's north woods. Flat needles with two white bands beneath, and blisters of fragrant resin on smooth grey bark.
A western fir with long, blue-grey needles that curve upward from the twig. Tolerates city conditions better than most firs.
A Pacific Northwest fir whose needles lie in flat, glossy ranks and smell strongly of citrus when crushed.
A dense, dark fir from the Caucasus, widely grown for Christmas trees because its needles hold on so stubbornly.
A small Asian maple with three-lobed leaves like a duck's foot and flaking, patchy bark on older trunks.
A compact European maple with small, blunt-lobed leaves and milky sap in the leaf stalk. Long used for hedging in Britain.
A shrubby maple from northeast Asia grown for its fiercely red autumn colour and fragrant spring flowers.
Cinnamon-coloured bark peels in papery curls year-round, making this small Chinese maple as striking in winter as in leaf.
An untidy, fast-growing native maple with compound leaves that look more like ash. Colonises riverbanks and disturbed ground.
The Japanese maple of gardens, with finely cut, star-shaped leaves and a layered, sculptural habit.
Widely planted street tree now considered invasive in the Northeast; shades out native seedlings.
A Norway maple selection whose leaves stay deep purple-black all summer. Invasive like the species, and heavily planted before that was understood.
One of the earliest trees to flower in spring; tolerant of wet soils.
Leaves flash silver-white beneath in a breeze, which is where the name comes from. Fast-growing and brittle, so old specimens often carry storm damage.
Vermont's state tree and the source of maple syrup. Brilliant orange to scarlet fall color.
A hybrid of red and silver maple that combines the red's autumn colour with the silver's speed. Nearly all campus specimens are named cultivars.
Big palmate leaves, candelabra flower spikes in May, and the glossy brown conkers that children have collected for centuries.
Among the first native trees to flower, in a haze of white before the leaves. The June berries are edible and much loved by birds.
A gawky, sparsely branched small tree armed with vicious prickles, carrying enormous compound leaves and frothy late-summer flower heads.
Bronze-gold shredding bark; twigs smell of wintergreen when scratched.
Dark, cherry-like bark and twigs that smell distinctly of wintergreen when scratched — the original source of the oil.
A river birch whose ragged, salmon-pink bark peels in sheets. Unusually heat-tolerant for a birch, and resistant to bronze birch borer.
White peeling bark makes this one of the most recognizable trees in Vermont.
A slender pioneer birch of poor soils, with chalky white bark that does not peel and dark triangular patches beneath each branch.
A Pacific coast cypress with drooping, curtain-like sprays of foliage that give it a permanently wilted look.
Smooth grey bark ripples over the trunk like flexed muscle, giving it the names musclewood and blue beech. An understory tree of moist woods.
A hickory of dry upland slopes, with compound leaves that turn clear gold and a thin-husked nut that squirrels open readily.
Enormous heart-shaped leaves, showy white flowers in June, and long bean-like pods that hang through winter.
Corky, warty ridges on the bark make this one easy to name by touch. Its small dark fruits persist into winter for the birds.
Round blue-green leaves turn apricot in autumn and give off a distinct smell of burnt sugar or cotton candy as they fall.
Magenta-pink flowers erupt directly from bare branches in spring, before the heart-shaped leaves appear.
The same Pacific coast cypress as Callitropsis nootkatensis under an older name — a species that has moved between genera repeatedly.
A Japanese cypress with fans of blunt, glossy foliage marked underneath by white Y-shaped lines. Sacred timber in Japan.
Japanese cypress grown in many forms, from feathery threadleaf cultivars to soft moss-like mounds.
Smooth grey bark like a beech, bright yellow autumn colour, and long chains of white pea flowers in early summer — though not every year.
Horizontal tiered branching gives this understory species its common name.
Four large white bracts surround the true flowers, opening before the leaves. Under pressure from dogwood anthracnose across its range.
A later-flowering Asian dogwood with pointed white bracts, raspberry-like fruit, and mottled bark on older trunks.
Clusters of small yellow flowers on bare twigs in very early spring, followed by tart red fruit used for preserves in eastern Europe.
Grown here as the contorted cultivar, whose twisted, corkscrewing branches are most striking once the leaves have dropped.
Airy plumes of spent flower stalks give the whole shrub a smoky haze through summer.
The American smoketree, rarer than its European cousin and better in autumn, when it turns brilliant orange and scarlet.
Thorny small trees with clustered white flowers and red haws. Notoriously difficult to identify to species, which is why the inventory stops at the genus.
Blocky, alligator-hide bark and orange fruit that stays mouth-puckeringly astringent until it is thoroughly ripe.
Narrow silver leaves and fragrant summer flowers, but an aggressive invader of open ground and riverbanks. Mapped so it can be removed.
Smooth gray bark; a keystone species now threatened by beech leaf disease.
The European beech, with the same smooth grey bark as the native species but usually a broader, lower crown. Purple-leaved forms are common.
Under severe pressure from emerald ash borer; campus specimens are monitored closely.
A tough, fast street tree now devastated across the region by emerald ash borer. Campus specimens are monitored closely.
A living fossil with fan-shaped leaves that turn uniform butter yellow.
Fine, ferny compound leaves cast a light dappled shade. Thornless forms dominate in planting; wild trees carry fearsome branched spines.
Fine dappled shade and no thorns; a workhorse of urban plantings.
Bare and gaunt for much of the year, hence the name. Huge doubly compound leaves emerge very late and drop very early.
White bell flowers dangle in rows beneath the branches in May, followed by curious four-winged dry fruits.
Deeply furrowed dark bark and aromatic compound leaves. Its roots release juglone, which suppresses many plants growing beneath it.
A variable Asian juniper carrying both needle-like juvenile and scale-like adult foliage, often on the same branch.
Junipers recorded without a species. Foliage may be needle-like, scale-like, or both, and the berry-like cones are actually fleshy scales.
Not a true cedar but a juniper, with shredding red-brown bark and dense blue berry-like cones. First tree to colonise old pastures.
A European larch: a conifer that turns gold and drops every needle each November, standing bare through winter.
A deciduous conifer whose needles turn gold and drop each November.
Star-shaped leaves turning every shade from yellow to deep purple, corky wings on the twigs, and spiky seed balls underfoot.
Straight-trunked and tall, with oddly squared-off leaves and greenish-orange tulip flowers held high in the crown where they are easily missed.
A small, tough legume from Manchuria with upright spikes of dull white flowers in midsummer, when little else is in bloom.
Thick, glossy evergreen leaves with rusty felt beneath and enormous fragrant white flowers. At the very cold edge of its range here.
Carries the largest simple leaves of any tree in North America — up to three feet long — and flowers to match.
A shrubby magnolia covered in many-petalled white stars in very early spring, often before the last frost catches them.
The familiar saucer magnolia, with large pink-and-white goblets opening on bare branches. A hybrid raised in France in the 1820s.
Deep pink spring bloom followed by small red fruit that persists into winter.
The orchard apple. Vermont's cider and dessert varieties all belong here, descended from wild apples of central Asia.
Ornamental crabapples, planted in dozens of named varieties for spring bloom and persistent fruit. Recorded without cultivar in the 2014 survey.
Known only as a fossil until living trees were found in China in the 1940s. A deciduous conifer with soft feathery needles that turn russet before falling.
Introduced for silkworm culture and now widely naturalised. Leaves vary wildly in shape on the same branch, and the fruit stains everything.
Glossy leaves that turn the most intense scarlet of any native tree, often starting in August. Horizontal branching gives it a tiered look.
Called ironwood for its extremely hard timber. Shreddy, cat-scratched bark and hop-like papery fruit clusters in late summer.
European spruce with drooping branchlets and very long cones.
A native northern spruce with stiff blue-green needles that smell unpleasantly of cat when crushed, earning it the name skunk spruce.
The blue spruce of front lawns, with rigid, viciously sharp needles and a strongly conical outline.
Spruces recorded without a species. All have short, stiff, four-sided needles set on small woody pegs that stay behind when a needle drops.
A dense, dark European pine with long stiff needles in pairs. Tolerant of salt and city air, so often planted along roads.
Needles in pairs snap cleanly when bent, which separates it from other native pines. Reddish plated bark and a straight, clean trunk.
Soft needles in bundles of five; the tallest tree in the Northeast forest.
Recognisable at a distance by the flaky orange bark of its upper trunk and its short, twisted blue-green needle pairs.
A hybrid plane tree whose bark flakes away in jigsaw patches of cream, olive and brown. Famously tolerant of polluted city air.
Sticky, aromatic buds scent the air in spring — the balm of Gilead. A northern species of river flats and cold ground.
A massive floodplain tree with coarsely toothed triangular leaves that clatter in wind, and cottony seed that drifts in early summer.
Planted as the Lombardy form, a narrow exclamation mark of a tree used for windbreaks and avenues. Short-lived and prone to canker.
Flattened leaf stalks make the foliage tremble in the slightest breeze.
Purple-leaved plum, grown for foliage rather than fruit. Pale pink flowers appear on bare twigs very early in spring.
Amur chokecherry, grown almost entirely for its glossy, peeling bark in polished amber and bronze.
A short-lived native cherry that floods in after fire or logging, then gives way as longer-lived trees close over it.
The Japanese flowering cherries, usually double-flowered and fruitless, planted purely for a brief and spectacular spring bloom.
Cherries and plums recorded without a species. All share horizontal lenticel bands across the bark and simple toothed leaves.
Higan cherry, often grown in weeping form, and among the earliest cherries to flower. Sometimes blooms again in a mild autumn.
The Yoshino cherry of Washington's Tidal Basin: pale blush flowers, almost white, opening all at once before the leaves.
Not a true fir. Its cones are unmistakable, with three-pointed bracts poking out between the scales like the hind legs of a mouse.
A small tree with three-part leaves and flat circular winged fruits like elm seeds, which is where the name wafer ash comes from.
Once planted everywhere for its neat shape and early white bloom, now regretted: the branches split in storms and it escapes into the wild.
The orchard pear, with glossy leaves, white spring flowers and blocky, checkered bark on old trunks.
Long-lived oak with distinctive rounded leaf lobes and pale bark.
A white oak of wet ground, with leaves dark green above and silvery beneath, and bark that flakes and curls on young branches.
Deeply cut, bristle-tipped leaves that turn brilliant scarlet late in the season and hold on well into winter.
A southern laurel oak with narrow, nearly untoothed leaves. Well outside its natural range here.
An oak with unlobed, laurel-like leaves that surprise anyone expecting an oak. Its wood was once split for roof shingles.
Enormous acorns in shaggy, fringed cups. Thick corky bark makes it the most fire-resistant oak of the prairie edge.
A southern bottomland oak with large, coarsely scalloped leaves and sweet acorns favoured by wildlife.
Chinkapin oak, with narrow chestnut-like leaves edged in sharp even teeth. Prefers limestone soils.
Lower branches sweep distinctly downward while the upper ones rise — a silhouette no other oak shares. Deeply cut leaves turn bronze-red.
Chestnut oak of dry rocky ridges, with deeply furrowed blocky bark and wavy-edged leaves. Now usually called Quercus montana.
The English oak of parkland and literature, with short-stalked leaves, long-stalked acorns, and a broad spreading crown when open-grown.
Fast-growing oak with acorns that feed campus squirrels and jays.
Inner bark is bright orange-yellow and was once used as a dye. Leaves are glossy above with rusty hairs in the vein axils beneath.
A Class B noxious weed in Vermont; mapped so that removal work can be tracked.
Deeply furrowed rope-like bark, paired thorns at each bud, and hanging chains of intensely fragrant white flowers in June.
A large European willow with narrow silvery leaves. Its wood is light, tough and shock-resistant.
Willows recorded without a species. They hybridise so freely that even specialists often stop at the genus.
Leaves come in three shapes on the same tree — oval, mitten and three-lobed — and everything about it smells of root beer when broken.
Rowan, or European mountain ash. Flat heads of white flowers give way to dense clusters of orange-red berries that birds strip quickly.
A hybrid mountain ash whose leaves are part-divided, part-whole — an obvious blend of its two parents.
White camellia-like flowers in midsummer and flaking bark in grey, orange and cinnamon. Good in every season.
A lilac that grows as a real tree, carrying huge plumes of creamy flowers in June, well after the shrubby lilacs have finished.
Intensely fragrant May bloom; a fixture of old Vermont dooryards.
A deciduous conifer of southern swamps whose feathery foliage turns rusty orange before dropping. Produces knobbly root knees in wet ground.
Northern white cedar, growing as flat sprays of scale-like foliage. Cliff-clinging wild trees in Vermont are among the oldest in eastern North America.
Arborvitae recorded without a species. Flattened fans of scale-like foliage and shreddy, fibrous bark.
Fragrant early-summer flowers that are heavily visited by bees.
Small neat heart-shaped leaves and intensely fragrant summer flowers that bees work all day. The standard European street linden.
A large-leaved linden that flowers earlier than the others, with softly hairy leaf undersides.
Leaves flash bright silver-white beneath as they turn in the wind. More tolerant of heat and drought than other lindens.
A natural hybrid of the small- and large-leaved lindens, long planted in European avenues. Often sprouts a thicket of shoots around its base.
Deeply shade-tolerant conifer of cool ravines; threatened by hemlock woolly adelgid.
The vase-shaped elm that once arched over American main streets, lost in vast numbers to Dutch elm disease. Survivors are worth protecting.
A Dutch elm disease-resistant selection used to restore the classic American elm vase form.
Wych elm, with very large rough-textured leaves that feel like sandpaper and a lopsided base typical of elms.
A tough, fast, brittle Asian elm planted for shelterbelts and now weedy across much of the continent.
Elms recorded without a species. All share doubly toothed leaves with a distinctly uneven base.
An elm relative planted as a disease-resistant substitute for the American elm, with a similar vase shape and flaking orange-grey bark.
